title: X-bar theory: bar levels, specifiers, complements and adjuncts
summary: See what Week 6's flat trees can't show, add the bar level (V′, N′) that 'do so' and 'one' actually replace, and use the X-bar template to tell a specifier, a complement and an adjunct apart by position. Draw X-bar trees for sentences with subjects, possessors and stacked adjuncts.
sourceNote: Week 7 handout 'X-bar theory' (Dr. Nie, (1) to (14)); Carnie, Syntax: A Generative Introduction ch. 6. Every tree here is generated from the handout's own rules, with all three levels (XP, X′, X) on every phrase as the handout asks. Oral Exam 1 territory.

sections.heading: Start here: what flat trees can't show

blocks.md: **The problem** Week 6's rules built **flat** phrases: a VP was just V followed by everything after it, all sisters. Dr. Nie's handout starts by testing that on one sentence, and it fails.
blocks.label: why

blocks.title: Handout (1)
blocks.body:
(1) Lee will circle the track extremely recklessly in the morning.

How many units can **do so** replace?

  a. Lee will circle the track extremely recklessly in the morning, and Sam will **do so** too.
     (do so = circle the track extremely recklessly in the morning)
  b. …, and Sam will **do so** in the evening.
     (do so = circle the track extremely recklessly)
  c. …, and Sam will **do so** carefully in the evening.
     (do so = circle the track)

Three different strings pass the test, so all three are constituents.

blocks.caption: The flat Week 6 tree for (1). Click the VP: it's the only node above *circle*. There is **no node** for *circle the track* or *circle the track extremely recklessly*, even though do so just proved both are units.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D ∅] [NP [N Lee]]] [T will] [VP [V circle] [DP [D the] [NP [N track]]] [AdvP [AdvP [Adv extremely]] [Adv recklessly]] [PP [P in] [DP [D the] [NP [N morning]]]]]]

columns: Can the flat tree show it?
rows: the phrase is named after it (VP ← V)
every other daughter of the phrase
the object DP and the adverb are both just sisters of V
the order of V and its complement
no node for *circle the track*, which do so proves is a unit
blocks.title: The handout's question: what can our diagrams represent so far?

blocks.md: **Why it matters** A theory of syntax should draw a node for every unit the tests find, and nothing else. The flat tree misses units and can't tell a complement from an adjunct, two things you already know are real from Weeks 4 and 5. X-bar theory fixes both with one idea: a middle layer.
blocks.label: why

sections.heading: Bar levels: the missing middle layer

blocks.body: An **intermediate projection** of a head: bigger than the head, smaller than the whole phrase. Read V′ as **'V-bar'**. A category has exactly **one head** and **one phrase level**, but it can have **several bar levels**.
The levels built on one head: the head V **projects** up to V′ and then to VP. They all share the head's category, which is why the phrase is named after its head.

blocks.md: **What do so really replaces.** The handout's point: do so substitution targets the **V-bar**, not the VP. Each do so in (1a) to (1c) replaced a different V′. So the VP needs one V′ per unit the test found.

rows: a VP is made of a V-bar
a V-bar can be another V-bar plus an adverb phrase or a PP after it
the lowest V-bar is the verb and its object
blocks.title: Handout (3): the flat VP rule, rewritten with bar levels

blocks.caption: Sentence (1) in X-bar form. Click each V′ from the bottom up: *circle the track*, then *circle the track extremely recklessly*, then everything including *in the morning*. Each one is exactly a string that do so replaced.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Lee]]]]] [T′ [T will] [VP [V′ [V′ [V′ [V circle] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N track]]]]]] [AdvP [Adv′ [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv extremely]]] [Adv′ [Adv recklessly]]]]] [PP [P′ [P in] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N morning]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.body: The rule V′ → V′ (AdvP / PP) has V′ on **both** sides of the arrow. That's on purpose: it can apply again to its own output, so adjuncts can stack without limit. It is recursion, from Week 1.

blocks.prompt: In (1), which string does the **lowest** V′ cover?
blocks.answer: *circle the track*: the verb and its object DP (the complement).

blocks.prompt: How many V′ nodes does (1) need, and why that number?
blocks.answer: **Three**: one for V + complement, and one more for each adjunct (*extremely recklessly*, *in the morning*). Each is a unit that do so can replace.

blocks.md: **One template for every phrase.** Instead of a different flat rule for each category, X-bar theory says every phrase, whatever its head (N, V, P, Adj, Adv, D, T), has the same shape. X stands for any category.

rows: a phrase on the left, under XP
X′ → ZP X′  or  X′ → X′ ZP
a phrase next to an X′, under an X′
a phrase next to the head

blocks.caption: The template drawn out. Hover each label for its definition. The three kinds of dependent are told apart purely by **where they attach**.

blocks.body: A phrase that is **sister to the head X** and a **daughter of X′**. (*the track* in *circle the track*.)
A phrase that is **sister to an X′** and a **daughter of an X′**. (*in the morning*.)
A phrase that is **sister to an X′** and a **daughter of the XP**. (The subject, as the next section shows.)

blocks.md: **Every phrase has all three levels, even alone.** The handout's (6): a phrase with just a head is still XP over X′ over X. *Lee* is a DP, *track* sits in an NP over an N′ over an N. Draw all three every time.

**Handout question: why can a head have only a few complements and specifiers, but unlimited adjuncts?** Look at which rules can repeat. X′ → X WP puts the head at the bottom, so it applies **once**: one set of complements. XP → YP X′ builds the top, so it also applies **once**: one specifier. X′ → X′ ZP has X′ on both sides, so it can apply **again and again**: unlimited adjuncts. The template's shape is the explanation.
blocks.label: think

blocks.prompt: A phrase is a daughter of V′ and a sister of V. What is it?
A phrase is a daughter of N′ and a sister of another N′. What is it?

blocks.body: The handout puts it in one line: the object DP is the complement of V, the VP is the complement of T, and **the subject DP is the specifier of T**. So TP → DP T′, and T′ → T VP.

blocks.caption: Handout (7): *Erin PRES plays her guitar in the evenings.* Click T′: it covers T and the whole VP. The subject *Erin* sits above it, as the specifier. *in the evenings* is an adjunct V′; *her guitar* is the complement of *plays*.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N Erin]]]]] [T′ [T PRES] [VP [V′ [V′ [V plays] [DP [D′ [D her] [NP [N′ [N guitar]]]]]] [PP [P′ [P in] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N evenings]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: Handout (8): *Her phone PAST buzzed loudly for several minutes.* *buzz* takes no object, so the lowest V′ is just the verb. Two adjuncts stack as two more V′ levels.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D her] [NP [N′ [N phone]]]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V′ [V′ [V buzzed]] [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv loudly]]]] [PP [P′ [P for] [DP [D′ [D several] [NP [N′ [N minutes]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.md: **DPs have specifiers too.** Handout (9) asks what category a possessive is. A possessive pronoun like *her* fills the **D** slot: it can't sit next to another determiner (`*the her phone` is out). A possessive **nominal** like *Michelle's* is different: *Michelle* is a whole DP, and *'s* is the D head.

rows: the possessor is the **specifier** of DP
's is the head; the thing possessed is its **complement** NP
blocks.title: Handout (10): possessors

blocks.caption: (9b) *Michelle's phone*: the possessor DP *Michelle* is the specifier, *'s* is D, and *phone* is the complement NP. Edit the brackets to try (9a) and (9c).

blocks.title: (9a) and (9c) in brackets
blocks.body:
(9a) her phone:
[DP [D′ [D her] [NP [N′ [N phone]]]]]

(9c) my best friend's phone:
[DP [DP [D′ [D my] [NP [N′ [N [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj best]]] [N′ [N friend]]]]]]]]] [D′ [D 's] [NP [N′ [N phone]]]]]

In (9c) the possessor is itself a DP with its own adjunct: *best* sits on an N′ inside it.

blocks.prompt: In *the artist's collection*, which phrase is the specifier of the DP, and what is D?
blocks.answer: *the artist* is the specifier (a possessor DP); D is *'s*.

blocks.prompt: What is the specifier of TP in *Erin plays her guitar*?

sections.heading: Inside the noun phrase: one targets N′

blocks.title: Handout (11)
blocks.body:
(11) those heavy sacks of flour in the corner

How many units can **one(s)** replace?

  a. those **ones** (= heavy sacks of flour in the corner)
  b. those **ones** in the corner (= heavy sacks of flour)
  c. those heavy **ones** in the corner (= sacks of flour)
  d. ✗ those heavy **ones** of flour in the corner (ones = sacks: FAILS)

Three units pass, and *sacks* alone does not.

blocks.md: **Same pattern as do so.** One substitution targets the **N-bar**, not the NP. And *of flour* can't be left behind (11d) because it is the **complement** of *sacks*: it's inside the lowest N′ with the head. *heavy* and *in the corner* are adjuncts, each adding an N′.

rows: a noun phrase is made of an N-bar
an N-bar can add an adjective before it or a PP after it (adjuncts)
the lowest N-bar is the noun and maybe its complement PP
blocks.title: Handout (12): NP rules in X-bar form

blocks.caption: (11) in X-bar form. Click the three N′ nodes: they are exactly (11c), (11b) and (11a). The PP *of flour* hangs from the lowest N′, next to the head: a complement.

params.bracket: [DP [D′ [D those] [NP [N′ [N [NP [N′ [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj heavy]]] [N′ [N sacks] [PP [P′ [P of] [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N flour]]]]]]]]] [PP [P′ [P in] [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N corner]]]]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: Handout (13): *the artist's rather ugly collection of paintings*. Possessor in the specifier, *of paintings* as the complement of *collection*, and *rather ugly* as an adjunct N′ (with *rather* as an adjunct inside the AdjP).

params.bracket: [DP [DP [D′ [D the] [NP [N′ [N artist]]]]] [D′ [D 's] [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [AdvP [Adv′ [Adv rather]]] [Adj′ [Adj ugly]]]] [N′ [N collection] [PP [P′ [P of] [DP [D′ [D ∅] [NP [N′ [N paintings]]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.md: **Handout (14) is ambiguous**, and X-bar shows exactly where: *She PAST tripped that unlucky man with a cane*. If she used the cane, *with a cane* is an adjunct on a **V′**. If the man had the cane, it's an adjunct on an **N′** inside the object.

blocks.caption: (14), reading A: she tripped him using a cane. The PP is an adjunct V′.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D she]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V′ [V tripped] [DP [D′ [D that] [NP [N′ [N [NP [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj unlucky]]] [N′ [N man]]]]]]]]]] [PP [P′ [P with] [DP [D′ [D a] [NP [N′ [N cane]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.caption: (14), reading B: the man who had a cane. The PP is an adjunct N′ inside the object DP.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D′ [D she]]] [T′ [T PAST] [VP [V′ [V tripped] [DP [D′ [D that] [NP [N′ [N [NP [N′ [N′ [AdjP [Adj′ [Adj unlucky]]] [N′ [N man]]] [PP [P′ [P with] [DP [D′ [D a] [NP [N′ [N cane]]]]]]]]]]]]]]]]]]

blocks.prompt: In *a student of physics with long hair*, which PP is on the lowest N′?
blocks.answer: *of physics*: it's the complement of *student*, sister to the head N. *with long hair* is an adjunct on a higher N′.

sections.heading: If this is your oral-exam concept

blocks.md:
- Definition: X-bar theory says every phrase has the same shape, XP over X′ over X, and dependents are named by where they attach.
- Why it's needed: flat trees miss units that do so and one prove exist, and can't tell complements from adjuncts.
- The three positions: complement = sister of the head; adjunct = sister of X′ under X′; specifier = sister of X′ under XP.
- The evidence: do so replaces V′, one replaces N′ (handout (1) and (11)).
- Why adjuncts are unlimited: X′ → X′ ZP can repeat; the complement and specifier rules can't.
- Live problem: 'Draw this sentence in X-bar and label every dependent.' Start from TP: subject in Spec,TP; T′ → T VP; complement next to V; one V′ per adjunct.

blocks.prompt: Say it out loud in one breath: why does X-bar theory need a bar level at all?
blocks.answer: Because do so and one replace strings that are bigger than a head but smaller than a phrase (*circle the track*, *sacks of flour*), so the tree needs a node there: the bar level.

rows: Week 6's trees: every dependent is a sister of the head.
A middle layer between the head and the phrase. One or more per phrase.
The head and the levels built on it: X, X′, XP.
XP → YP X′; X′ → X′ ZP (or ZP X′); X′ → X WP.
Sister of the head, daughter of X′.
Sister of X′, daughter of X′. Can stack.
Sister of X′, daughter of XP. The subject is Spec of TP.
A DP in the specifier of a DP headed by 's.

exercises.title: Count the N′s
exercises.prompt: How many N′ nodes does 'those heavy sacks of flour in the corner' have in X-bar form?
hints: One N′ for the head and its complement.
The adjuncts are 'heavy' and 'in the corner'.
solution: **3**: [sacks of flour], [heavy sacks of flour], [heavy sacks of flour in the corner]. Each is replaceable by one(s).
